landmark_rows.label: Devil's Arrows
landmark_rows.note: The name is mentioned by John Aubrey, who visited and drew the stones in 1687; a legend that the Devil threw the stones at Aldborough goes back to 1721. The stones were erected in the Stone Age.

landmark_rows.label: Devil's Dyke
landmark_rows.note: Used as a defensive site before and after the Iron Age (Atlas of Hillforts: Devil's Dyke, Poynings). Legend: the Devil dug a trench through the Downs so that the sea would drown the Christians of the Weald; St Cuthman of Steyning fooled him with a candle and a crowing cock, and he fled, leaving the dyke unfinished.

landmark_rows.label: Devil's Bridge
landmark_rows.note: The first mention of the structure using the English name Devil's Bridge, in historical records, is from 1734.

landmark_rows.label: Devil's Jumps
landmark_rows.note: The first mention of the Devil's Jumps appears to be on a map by John Rocque, dating to 1765. Legend: the Devil leapt from hill to hill until Thor threw a boulder at him.

landmark_rows.label: Devil's Dyke
landmark_rows.note: In medieval times it was simply called the dic (the ditch), le Micheldyche or magnum fossatum (great ditch). Thought most likely Anglo-Saxon, by analogy with Fleam Dyke (AD 330 to 510).

landmark_rows.label: Devil's Punch Bowl
landmark_rows.note: Legend: the Devil hurled lumps of earth at Thor, or Thor at the Devil, leaving the hollow.
